content: Participants in the Nurses’ Health Study (NHS) initiated in 1976 included 121,701 female nurses aged 30 to 55 years from 11 U.S. states, who completed a self-administered, mailed questionnaire. Similarly, the Nurses’ Health Study II (NHS II), launched in 1989, involved 116,671 female nurses aged 25 to 42 years. A total of 149,693 parous women were enrolled to investigate the impact of breastfeeding (BF) on ovarian cancer risk. Women with a prior cancer diagnosis, those who had died before the study baseline, and other exclusions were not included. Breastfeeding duration was analyzed categorically in six-month increments (e.g., 0, 1–6, 7–11, 12–17, 18+ months). The primary outcome was the risk of ovarian cancer. The UK Women’s Cohort Study (UKWCS) collected data in two phases (1995–1998 and 1999–2002) from 61,000 women at baseline and 12,453 in the second phase. The study analyzed the relationship between lifetime breastfeeding duration and breast cancer risk, identifying 1,762 incident breast cancer cases. The mean age at recruitment was 54 years, and women with cancer at enrollment were excluded. The Cebu Longitudinal Health and Nutrition Survey in the Philippines collected data on all pregnant women in 33 randomly selected barangays of Metropolitan Cebu who gave birth between May 1983 and April 1984. The study examined infant feeding patterns, factors influencing feeding decisions, and their health, nutritional, demographic, and economic implications. Breastfeeding data were collected at birth and every two months until 24 months. Breastfeeding duration was defined as the age at which the infant stopped breastfeeding or the last known breastfeeding age if it exceeded 24 months. Exclusion criteria included nulliparity, no breastfeeding, premature ovarian failure, smoking, and chronic diseases or medications affecting bone mass. Breastfeeding duration for each child was obtained through detailed interviews. A cross-sectional study in São Paulo, Brazil, evaluated children aged 6 to 14 years enrolled in a private school. Mothers completed a structured questionnaire on breastfeeding occurrence and duration, categorized as never breastfed, <3 months, 3–5 months, 6–11 months, and >12 months. The study assessed obesity in children and adolescents. The SMILE (Study of Mothers’ and Infants’ Life Events) birth cohort in Adelaide, South Australia, recruited 2,147 mothers and 2,181 children between July 2013 and August 2014. Participants completed questionnaires at recruitment and follow-ups at 3, 6, 12, and 24 months. Breastfeeding duration was determined based on whether the child was still receiving breast milk and, if not, the age at cessation. The Early Childhood Development Project in the Philippines followed children aged 0–4 years in disadvantaged municipalities. Breastfeeding duration was assessed through maternal recall during annual follow-ups, and children were categorized into five groups based on breastfeeding duration (e.g., 0–5 months, 6–11 months, etc.). A study in Turkey included postmenopausal women over 40 years of age who attended osteoporosis outpatient clinics. Exclusion criteria included active gastrointestinal or liver disease, renal failure, malignancy, and medications affecting bone metabolism. Exclusions included non-response to questionnaires, current pregnancy, age above 85 years, and unknown lactation history. Lifetime lactation duration was categorized into five levels (e.g., none, 1–6 months, etc.), and cardiovascular mortality was assessed through linkage with the Cause of Death Registry. A study in North Carolina recruited women aged 40–54 years through advertisements. Inclusion criteria required at least one intact ovary and no physical impairments. The Christchurch Child Development Study in New Zealand followed infants born in 1977 through structured interviews with mothers. Breastfeeding duration was classified into categories such as totally bottle-fed, breastfed for <4 months, and breastfed for ≥12 months. A study in Porto, Portugal, included children aged 5–10 years randomly selected from elementary schools. Parents completed questionnaires on sociodemographic characteristics, asthma, and breastfeeding. Asthma was defined as self-reported and physician-diagnosed. The Pelotas Birth Cohort in Brazil followed 5,304 children born in 1993. The Encuesta Longitudinal de la Primera Infancia (ELPI) cohort in Chile included children aged 7–24 months with complete data on confounders. Breastfeeding duration was categorized into four groups (e.g., never breastfed, breastfed up to 6 months, etc.), and behavioral problems were assessed using the CBCL 1½–5 parent report. The CDC Pediatric Nutrition Surveillance System aggregated data on low-income children attending public health clinics. Breastfeeding duration was analyzed in relation to growth and anemia outcomes.
